name: Readiness Estimates
title: Readiness Estimates
answer: Readiness estimates are predictions drawn from benchmark results about which students are likely to pass state tests. They matter because they give teachers a signal early enough to target support before the test, but they are predictions and carry real uncertainty. A student estimated as likely to fail is not destined to fail.

crumbs.name: Assessment, Data, and the Early Warning System

sections.body: Many districts use benchmark results to estimate which students are likely to pass state tests. These estimates help teachers aim support at the right students before the test happens. The problem they solve is timing, because waiting for the test itself leaves no room to act. At the same time, they are predictions, with all the uncertainty that comes with forecasting. The estimate is a starting point for adult planning, not a verdict on a student.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: Teachers should review readiness estimates rather than accept them as they arrive. A teacher might know that a student had a bad testing day, or that another student has recently made big gains. That knowledge adds context the data does not contain on its own. The final list of students chosen for extra support should reflect both the estimate and what the teacher knows. The text does not give grade bands for this practice, so it applies wherever benchmark results are used to plan support.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text supplies no study, figure or finding for readiness estimates. This idea rests on practice rather than research. The only support it offers is the chapter's own account of uncertainty in predictions, which is a caution rather than a piece of evidence.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Readiness estimates should never be shared with students as labels. Telling a student they are predicted to fail can discourage them. The estimate is a tool for adults to plan support, not a message for the student. Students should hear about their strengths and specific next steps instead of predictions. The decision about which students receive extra support stays with the teacher and the school, made with both the data and human judgment in view.
